tracks.title: Your DAG runs single-file
tracks.text: Lesson eight point five — waves. A sub-lesson, under workflows. The parent showed a board clearing in three rounds, and an org file compiling into a world. But rounds sounds sequential. And every orchestrator you have ever used taught you the same lie — that parallelism is something you configure. Airflow has executors and pools. GitHub Actions has runners and concurrency groups. Step Functions has Map states. So a fair suspicion walks in with you… the plan executes probably means a loop runs the tasks one at a time. [curious] It doesn't. And the reason is the most satisfying kind — no trick, just a definition you already had the pieces for. The dependency edges you wrote — one component's out feeding another's in — are already the concurrency declaration. Nothing else is needed… because nothing else is true.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. A wave is the set of steps whose predecessors are all done… executed at the same time. A compiled world clears in waves, not rounds. Wave N is everything that became ready once wave N minus one finished. The word matters. Round implies a turn taken by one actor. A wave is the opposite — a whole front advancing together. [excited] And the executor that does this lives in two functions… about seventy lines of Elixir, total. No queue. No broker. No worker pool. No scheduler config. The plan file is the spec, and the engine reads it.

tracks.title: Computing the waves
tracks.text: Now — computing the waves. Here is the entire scheduler in plain English. First, take the world's edges and group them by consumer, so each step knows its predecessors. Second, peel — a wave is every remaining step whose predecessors are all in the done set. Third, run that wave, add its steps to done, and peel again. And finally, when nothing remains, stop. That's it. Picture a five-step world. fetch and seed depend on nothing. clean consumes fetch. score consumes both clean and seed. report consumes score. Now watch it fall into bands. Wave one is the green pair — fetch and seed, no predecessors, so they go at once. Wave two is clean, alone — fetch is done, so clean is ready… but score can't move, because seed and clean aren't both finished yet. Wave three is score — now both its predecessors are done. Wave four is report. [curious] And here is the quiet thing. Nobody wrote that order. It fell out of the edges. And notice seed — it took a free seat way back in wave one, even though score wouldn't need it until wave three. The wave engine spends idle capacity the instant a step is eligible… not the instant it's strictly required.

tracks.title: The accumulator is the pipe
tracks.text: Next — the accumulator is the pipe. Within a wave, steps run. Between waves, data flows. And the mechanism is almost too plain to call a mechanism. The executor keeps one map — name to output. Each step's result lands in it, under the step's name. When the next step runs, it looks up its single producer in that map, and receives that string as its standard input. The map is the pipe. Picture a two-step world. Upper uppercases its input. Count reports the length of Upper's result. Follow it. The input — the words hello world — reaches Upper, because Upper is a root… it has no inbound edge, so it gets the workflow's original input. Upper writes a little record — upper, HELLO WORLD — into the map under its own name. Count has one inbound edge from Upper… so its input is exactly that string. Eleven characters, once uppercased. And Count writes its own record — len, eleven. Upper's stdout literally was Count's stdin. Two steps… two waves… one pipe. [curious] And one sharp limit lives right here. A component has at most one inbound edge. So fan-in isn't expressible — a step can't read two producers at once. But fan-out is free. Many components can name the same producer's output… and every one of them receives that single result.

tracks.title: Eight at a time
tracks.text: A depth rung — eight at a time. A wave runs through an async stream, with a concurrency of eight, and a per-slot timeout of ten minutes. So at most eight steps of a wave run truly in parallel. A wider wave queues the rest behind those eight. And the ten-minute slot is generous on purpose — it has to cover an agent thinking, or a component compiling in the sandbox for the very first time. But each individual wasm step lives under a much tighter budget than the wave that holds it. Picture the cap stack — six limits, each guarding something different. First, wave concurrency — eight at once — guards the shared engine, so a wide wave can't stampede the box. Second, the wave-slot timeout — ten minutes — guards the orchestration, covering agent thinking and first compiles. Third, the wasm step timeout — thirty seconds — guards one component, so a tight filter can't spin forever. Fourth, the fuel cap — five billion units — bounds the work even under the time cap. Fifth, the stdin cap — sixty-four mebibytes — guards memory, rejecting an oversized pipe instead of running out of it. And sixth, the argv cap — two hundred fifty-six kibibytes — keeps the launch path bounded. The verdict, in one line — a compiled filter gets thirty seconds and five billion fuel… while the slot holding it gets ten minutes, because that slot might instead be holding an agent, or a step compiling itself from source for the first time. [curious] And these are constants in the engine — not knobs you set per workflow. A real limitation. It's in the honest part too.

tracks.title: Agents in the DAG
tracks.text: Now the second aha — agents in the graph — and it costs the engine nothing. A step's language is usually a compiler target. JavaScript… Rust… Zig. But one language is special — agent. When a component's source block is tagged agent, the source block is the system prompt… and the piped input is the task. The step runs a full agent — model, tools, the loop — with a budget of six steps. And its final answer is the step's output, slotted into the same map as any compiled filter. [excited] Here's the trick. The wave engine doesn't know agents exist. It takes a step function. Inject the pure-wasm runner, and you get a compiler pipeline. Inject the agent-aware one, and the same scheduler fans out language models. So… run three sub-agents in parallel needs no new construct. It's three agent components with no edges between them. No edges means no predecessors… which means one wave… which means simultaneous. Picture two analysts on one topic — the safety of modern nuclear power. Read the org aloud. A workflow headline — Research fan-out. Under it, a component named Fact, with a source block tagged agent — you are a concise analyst, your task is a topic, reply with one key fact. And a second component named Risk — you are a concise risk analyst, reply with one key risk. Nothing joins them. Both nodes are green — same wave. Fact and Risk each get the topic as their task, run their own loop at the same time under the eight-wide limit, and land as two entries in the results. This is the brandnana-style sub-agent fan-out… expressed as two headlines in a plan file. One more detail — an agent step gets six steps of its own loop, where a standalone agent gets twelve. A workflow fans out many, so each is kept lean. And the agent in a wave has the same tools any agent has — an in-wasm shell, the virtual filesystem, the wb command line, the ability to file an issue. No native exec. The agent is a step… not an escape.

tracks.title: Why wave two is instant
tracks.text: A depth rung — why wave two is instant. Run the same world twice, and the second run is dramatically faster, for two reasons sitting underneath the wave engine. First, the build cache is content-addressed. A component's source hashes to a filename, and identical source returns the already-built wasm, tagged cached — no recompile. Second, the wasmtime compilation cache remembers the machine code wasmtime generated from that module… so a cached run skips the just-in-time compile entirely. And that second cache has a war story. Without it, every run compiled the module from scratch — which on a throttled shared core took minutes. The symptom looked like the wasm shell hangs. The cause was recompilation… every single time. Turning the cache on was the fix. Picture the difference as a small table. On the first run, the build is a full compile in the sandbox, and the run is a full just-in-time from scratch — both slow. On a repeat run, the build is a cache hit, and the run skips the just-in-time — both nearly free. [excited] The verdict — a wave's first pass pays for compilation… every pass after pays almost nothing. That's why the ten-minute slot exists at all. It's sized for that expensive first compile, not for steady state. In steady state, the same wave is gone in a blink.

tracks.title: What comes back
tracks.text: Next — what comes back. A run returns a record, not a log. For each workflow it's a map — the workflow name, its schedule, the world's exports, a tasks map of name to output, and a list of sub-workflows. Nested workflow headlines recurse — each sub-world runs its own waves and produces its own record. Picture a real Pipeline result. The workflow is Pipeline. Its tasks map has two entries — Upper holds the record upper, HELLO WORLD… and Count holds the record len, eleven. And there's one sub-workflow — Audit — whose single step Echo holds audited colon hello world. Two facts in that record earn their place. First — Upper's stdout literally was Count's stdin. The pipe, visible in the output. And second — the sub-workflow Audit ran its Echo step on audited hello world… which proves a sharp boundary. Sub-workflows receive the original top-level input… not the parent's outputs. Edges never cross a workflow boundary. A sub-world is a fresh run with the same input — not a downstream consumer of the parent. And you reach all of this over HTTP. Post to slash api slash workflow, with an org string and an input, and you get the records back. Add the plan flag, and you get the schedules and task names without executing — a dry run of the plan. Nothing runs.

tracks.title: Where it bites
tracks.text: Now the honest part — where it bites. The wave model is small and sharp… and sharp edges cut. First — no fan-in. A component has one optional in, so a step can't read two producers. If C needs both A and B, you can't wire it directly — you add a downstream merge step, or you wait for a typed composition path. Fan-out is free. Fan-in is a feature that isn't here yet. Second — errors flow as values. A failed step doesn't halt the wave. Its task value becomes an error tuple, and the run completes. That's a feature, until it isn't — a consumer downstream of a failed producer receives that error tuple as its input, which is non-binary, which the wasm lane rejects. And today it rejects it with a misleading input-too-large label… even when the real cause is the poisoned upstream. The error propagates. The label lies. We'd rather you knew. Third — cycles aren't validated. Validation checks two things — a component with no source, and an input with no upstream producer. It does not check for cycles. When the executor can't find any ready step but steps remain, it lumps all the survivors into one final wave and runs them at once with empty input… which the wasm lane rejects. So a cycle doesn't deadlock or hang. It degenerates into a final all-at-once wave that fails at the input guard. No hang… but a confusing failure, rather than a clean — you have a cycle. And fourth — the constants are constants. Eight-wide concurrency, the ten-minute slot, the thirty-second step timeout — none are per-workflow knobs today. And sub-workflows getting the original input is a real constraint, not a bug.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] How do I run two agents in parallel? Omit the edges. Two agent components with no in pointing at each other have no predecessors, so they land in the same wave and run at once. Parallelism is the absence of a dependency… not a flag. What if a step hangs? Two nets catch it. A wasm step has a thirty-second timeout and a five-billion fuel cap. The wave slot has a ten-minute ceiling above that. Either way the step's value becomes an error tuple, the run completes, and the failure is data. Can step C read both A and B? Not directly — a component has exactly one inbound edge. To merge two producers, add a downstream step, or restructure so one producer carries the merged payload. Is this just Airflow? No broker… no worker pool… no executor config. The plan file is the spec, and seventy lines of Elixir run it. The whole orchestration module is fifty lines — there isn't room for an Airflow in it. And — does the schedule fire the workflow on its own? [curious] The schedule is surfaced in the plan and the record — you can read every day at six off it. But autonomous firing is the keeper tier… not a cron loop hidden in the wave engine. Treat the schedule as declared intent that a keeper acts on.

tracks.title: Back up to the parent
tracks.text: So that's waves. The aha was simple. Parallelism here isn't configured — it's computed, from the edges you already wrote. The executor partitions a world into topological waves, runs each wave at once, and pipes producer to consumer through one map. Agents are just another step kind. And about seventy lines do the whole thing. [curious] The way back up is short. Workflows — lesson eight — is the parent, where rounds become waves. And worlds is the sibling that emits what these waves run. Everything here was built on the plan you already wrote.
